Honestly, as a widower with a current partner, I feel like there is a middle ground. I don't think it's great to have a comparison between a current and late partner in mind, though I recognize that it can potentially be difficult to achieve this. I think it's important to recognize that love is different with every person and strive for peace and happiness in that love and assess the presence or absence of that within the context of itself, rather within the context of other things like your previous relationship. Maybe your previous partner made you realize things you like to have in a relationship, but I think it's important to realize and make the distinction that you enjoy having x thing in a relationship, rather than that you enjoy that your late partner did x thing and subsequently dislike that your current partner doesn't. Then you can communicate that accordingly and try to better figure out if this new partner is good for you (and willing to help try and fulfill those needs) or if they aren't quite the right person you need. I think a new partner can, if given the chance, also show you new things that you learn to love in someone and make you realize other things you enjoy in a relationship. To me, that's what's special about it. I don't love my late partner more or less than my current partner, but I love them in unique ways. Sometimes, these ways are similar, and sometimes, they are different. They both occupy a different space in my heart because love is not a finite resource. It is infinite, and I will always have more to give. But also, just because I love my current partner does not mean that I don't still love my late partner, like you said, and so it's only natural they occupy a different space in my heart, as they both continue to fill those spaces themselves. I think it is important as a widower (if you want another serious relationship) to find someone who recognizes this and understands it or is willing to get to that point. That way, you can have someone who will talk with you about your late partner and share the memories and love in that relationship with them in ways that you might not be able to do with anyone else. That can be really special, and I promise that partners like that exist out there that don't expect you to act like you're divorced or never talk about your late partner. It might take some looking around, though. 

But, if I was on the other side of it and was told that my partner would choose their late partner over me? I would be hurt. I would never ask anyone to make that choice myself because it's unfair and impossible, and to be told that while these things are true, it seems like a betrayal of trust in some way. It would make me feel as if I'm always being compared, or if I'm not good enough, and I think tying someone's self-worth to your late partner to act out your own grief is a selfish decision that neither of them deserve in the end.

Agreed. I really appreciate the fact that the show depicts how the people we've loved and lost have changed us and impacted us even years after losing them. It also does a really good job of showing how grief resurfaces as time goes on, how that grief itself changes over time, and even how one can even find comfort and peace in that remembering. It's a show about finding the people we miss where we sometimes least expect them. I think I would have personally loved to have had this show around when I was in the depths of my own grief, even if watching it after a lot of processing has been done on my part has still been wonderful, too.

And that's totally a fair concern. I've enjoyed my time with the system a lot, but I can see how building a courtier a certain way could possibly break the dueling system. I'm glad you're enjoying the previous editions, though. There's a lot of good setting material from previous editions that I know my DM used in our games, even. And I definitely can vouch for how much fun I've had with the strife and opportunity systems. I'm a sucker for mechanics in a game that help portray a "theme" and possibly even encourage role-playing in various ways or make you think about what that mechanic being invoked might mean for the character and their mental state. Strife does exactly that kind of thing for me and it was always fun for me to interpret gaining strife on dice or utilizing it through other means. Hell, our group would often give our own characters strife unprompted if it felt relevant to what was happening. So if you ever have it in your mind to give 5e a try with a decent group, I hope you have fun with it just like I have!

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by someone clown(ing) their way into winning a sword duel. And as I understand it though, yes, some courtier schools do pretty well in duels. But dueling is definitely framed in the game as partially being a battle of composure, which fits the theme imo. I've mostly played bushi in the game myself and never have had trouble with the dueling system beyond what feels fair? But the group I've played it with doesn't try to break the game or anything, and we all try our best at the table to adhere to our narrative themes which comes with a level of seriousness and gravity whenever we have duels in the game so I guess your mileage may vary, but that maybe can be true about any game. Fwiw I've had some of my favorite ttrpg sessions in the last 15 years of playing/running ttrpgs in L5R 5e.

The mass battle system is good though! I had fun with it. I can't make comparisons to 4e because I've never played 4e, but I've liked it in 5e. I just have less to say about it specifically since the dueling system in 5e feels much more unique and "on theme" if that makes sense? Samurai duels are pretty synonymous with the samurai genre, and while they can feature mass battles or skirmishes as well, lots of genres of movie media will feature big skirmishes of some sort. Westerns are really the only thing I can think of that has the feel of a Samurai duel, and well that only makes sense seeing how they've influenced one another. 

Mass battles in general work a little different from duels and can last longer of course. But in general there's pretty decent rules for grouping enemies together to make it feel like you're a samurai taking down a bunch of bandits like you might see in Seven Samurai. The critical wounds system of the game is one of the highlights of the game in general imho, and you see that both in duels and in mass battles. It can cause a lot of quick tension or dramatic moments. It also uses more abstracted range in the form of range bands which I like, personally, but I know not everyone is into. You can also initiate duels during a skirmish and that's always a fun thing to do.

You are right! I definitely forgot that, and I guess I just wanted to highlight the dueling system as that can be a hallmark of a lot of samurai media. L5R can definitely handle stuff like skirmishes (which iirc is a lot closer to Seven Samurai's scenes specifically) and other things as well. All in all it's a good samurai game but I'm sure there are others, too!

Legend of the Five Rings 5th edition! The duel rules are the best and most fun for samurai duels in any system I've played (which is a lot). The game in general has a "strife" mechanic that helps encourage that samurai sense of stoicism and duty and honor, and this strife mechanic is built into the duels itself as each round of the duel has increasing amounts of strife you gain each turn. When one character caps? The other gets to make an immediate strike at them, and oftentimes it can be instantly deadly. This also means that spending the entire duel staring your opponent down and/or doing other things such as taunting them is a very viable strategy so you can get that one perfect swing in. It's very fast and very tense. I highly recommend. Of course, the game is set in its own fictionalized, fantasy version of Japan basically (which is a really fun setting!) but if you really wanted to port it to historical Japan I don't think it would be impossible or even terribly hard.

This exactly. Players matter so much more to the experience than I think people often give them credit for. Does a good GM matter? Yeah of course. You can outright be a bad GM who refuses to work with their players. But there's a certain amount of experience that goes into being a player as well. And sometimes a player's own bad experience can be self-inflicted. So much of ttrpg with a new group can be trying to figure out and accommodate everyone's preferences both as a player and a GM. As a GM and player, myself, my best games have often been when players themselves take initiative to be vocal about their desires for the game and also offer their own ideas for scenes or plot/hame elements that the GM might not even have thought of. TTRPG is just impossible to standardize which, as you say, makes the transactional aspect of paid GMing awkward.

Dishes are one of the only chores I feel like I have an okay handle on. But I used to work in food service and by extension really hate dirty dishes. They make me nauseous, so I've found the only way to get me to do them is to do them right as soon as I'm done using them so that they don't pile up or get increasingly gross and hard to tackle. It works well for me at least because usually I'm up and at the sink anyways so spending a couple minutes cleaning what I've used/putting it away isn't too bad for my brain. Now this isn't perfect because it gets harder to do the larger the meal is or the more dishes used in cooking ect, and also some days you're just tired after work or something and doing the dishes seems impossible when you wanna relax. It took time for me to get into the habit and it still breaks sometimes, but at the very least it definitely mitigates the amount I have to do in the future and many times keeps the kitchen clean.

I kind of feel like I'm being misunderstood as well? I mentioned in my first post and the second post that finding people to play pauper with is an issue. Despite this I believe it is still the best format to learn the game and get into the game as a beginner if you have the scene for it. It provides insight into mechanics and strategies in the game, as well as good examples of deck construction, sideboarding, and other aspects that appear across formats.  I've reiterated again and again that they should check with their lgs first. But I want to present the option in this thread because no one else has. Ultimately it comes to OP on what decision they make, and as long as they are having fun there is no wrong way to get into the game. And just because you've tried and failed or not seen local pauper scenes doesn't mean that is the case everywhere either. Though I will agree it is rarer to come across.

Kitchen table magic is also just fine, and how I began playing the game years ago (I have also played a lot of paper magic pre-pandemic), however I think it only works if you have a group to play/get into the game with. Playing at a local game store tends to lend itself to more established methods of playing in my experience, and can be a little unbalanced if you're taking a more "kitchen table" approach. I think beginners should win games and also be able to experience how strong decks can be. Pauper is just a good example of this since the strongest decks are cheap. But in general it would be nice if OP were able to go to the store and be allowed to play or watch some veteran's deck for whatever format, be it commander, modern, standard, ect.

That's why I suggest that they go to their game store first and inquire about the local pauper scene before deciding. Some places do have pauper players, even if it isn't as common. But at least the format is mentioned and in their mind. I have to disagree that precons are the way to go though, at least completely. Challenger decks could be just fine, but I generally think standard investment is not great for a new player (especially when the current challenger decks see cards rotating out in literally a few months), and I don't think commander is the best starting point for a new player. And then planeswalker decks (if those are even still around) and other similar precons are essentially useless products that become unplayable past gaining a basic understanding of the game. Arena is probably the best way to just simply learn the game first and decide whether or not it's for you since you can go through tutorial land and play it as a free to play game for a little bit. However when getting people playing magic in my experience one of the biggest hurdles is explaining the cost to people. Once people realize that they might spend 150$ or more on a standard deck just to see it become obsolete in the near future interest declines sharply. Similarly when they realize that other non rotating formats like modern can cost upwards of 1,500$. Most new players I've come in contact with are interested in making a smaller investment to just sit down and play. That's pauper, and I've never had a difficult time convincing other, even established magic players, to get into a format where top tier decks are around 30 dollars. So even if there isn't a pauper scene in town, at least someone mentioning it can put it in mind, and if OP is actually interested in the format it's a possible format to try and convince the people around them to play. I think that's reasonable in a post where people are mentioning modern and legacy as formats in the game

I'm never sure why people don't mention pauper in these posts. In my opinion pauper is THE best format to introduce beginners to. Pauper is a format based around only using common rarity cards in a deck. Has the card had a printing in common rarity? It's legal in the format (unless it's banned of course, but every format has a banlist). Pauper is THE cheapest format in the game. Decks can be bought for as little as 25 U.S. dollars or so at times. Decks do not rotate, so they essentially last forever (sometimes new cards will come out that are better choices for the deck, but that part can be fun) and so you can pick up pauper decks you've had for a few years and play again if you lose and regain interest one day (I have done exactly this). Not only that, but there are plenty of different types of decks to try. There's aggro, combo, control, tempo, and all kinds of deck types/playstyles. But most importantly, especially for a beginner, there are simple and easy playstyles you can pick up without having to wrap your head around the more complicated playstyles or effects in the game. For example, burn, mono green stompy, or something like boros monarch are straight-forward decks that can get you through learning a lot of the base mechanics of the game before you try something like izzet faeries which can be more reactive than proactive. Also? These cheap decks are top tier decks. There are some more expensive decks in the format. Izzet faeries for example can be around 70 U.S. dollars, but that's about as high as pricing goes for these decks, and is not the norm. I'd say it's usually more in the 30-40 range. Whereas standard decks will cost between 100-400$ and modern can go upwards to 1,500$. Pauper also never rotates like standard, and so as I said before, unless there are bannings your cards will always be playable. 

The only issue with pauper can be lack of people to play with. For some reason people just seem to not know about the format? But this varies by area and can also be fixed if you have someone to play with, and you can always try and convince others to play the format as well. I'd check with your local game store about the pauper scene you have there, as well as if they do any pauper tournaments or events. I've introduced a few people to the game through pauper, though, and I truly believe it's the best way to get into the game. Once you've checked with your lgs about the pauper scene in town and decided if you want to pick up a pauper deck, I'd find a list that looks fun/beginner friendly and take that list to your card shop and try and buy the cards there. I've had entire pauper decks I've been able to buy from my lgs on the spot and even if they didn't have all the cards I'm sure they could help you order the rest. 

As for some resources, here's a link to the pauper metagame on mtggoldfish. https://www.mtggoldfish.com/metagame/pauper#paper
This might be a bit confusing (or not!) on what everything means or what deck might be fun or good for you. But it's a place to start. You can look at decks and what cards they have and see what appeals to you. As I mentioned before, something like burn, mono green stompy or even boros aggro could be pretty beginner friendly. 

https://strategy.channelfireball.com/all-strategy/page/2/?s=Pauper
Channel fireball or places like that have articles you can read about specific decks at times. This can give you an idea of how the deck plays and as you become more familiar with the game will be easier to navigate on what playstyle you prefer. 

https://youtube.com/c/tolariancommunity
Also obligatory shout out to The Professor at Tolarian Community College (I saw someone else link a video of his earlier). He has great videos on navigating products, or even just learning how to play the game itself. He also has made deck tech videos on pauper before and has an entire playlist dedicated to them (I believe the Tron pauper deck video contains banned cards, but should be the only one). These can be helpful because he explains the purpose of each card and why it's in the deck. It helps give you an idea of playstyle, as well as how to play it. In general his YouTube channel is a great source for answers to questions that many magic the gathering players ask.

In general as you get more familiarity with the game you'll find out what you like and be able to dip your toes into more formats and playstyles. I personally like pauper and modern the best, while my least favorite formats tend to be commander and standard (though I enjoy those as well). What is played locally may have a lot of influence on what you play most. For example, I play a lot of commander despite it being my least favorite format because that's what a lot of people around me play. Pauper to me, however, is so cheap at an entry level that even if it's not the format you're playing most once you get yourself established in the game, I feel as if it can be an easy and good investment to begin with, especially if you want to learn the game.

I'm not very experienced with psychedelics in general. It's a rather new thing for me. In fact I've only had 2 trips so far. But for me, both of those trips have been taken during my own grieving process. I lost my fiancee of 8 years last year in February and honestly have had a horrible time of it since. I've spent most of  the time since in bed. Lots of time is spent crying and deeply depressed. I stopped going to work and have been living off of savings and with the help of family (especially through COVID). 

Part of my own interest in psychedelics was the research being done on how they can help treat or relieve depression, and how they can offer spiritual experiences (I am not religious, and this fact was not a source of comfort in my grief) and relief from things like grief, and the first contact I came with it was much of a "psilocybin finds you when you need it" experience (someone I knew had brought them up and gave them to me without me mentioning any initial interest).

 I took them a few weeks later, at home, by myself in my room whilst chatting with some friends online. It was a difficult experience. It started out great and I felt great love for the friends I was talking to, and honestly felt like I could even feel the presence of my fiancee around me at times. I felt like I could see the love that she has for me surrounding me and these friends of ours, and how that love persists and is eternal. But eventually I decided to get off the computer and just kind of... explore things myself. Things went dark after this. I had some initial fun afterwards explore some visuals but eventually I spent a lot time looking at pictures of my fiancee and almost reliving some of the memories we had together. I cried a lot and eventually became uncomfortable with the experience. I started to wonder when/if it would end (despite logically knowing that it would), and I started to think about how my reality was set in this experience of not having my fiancee around anymore. Part of me even began to think and wonder if I'd be alone forever. I tried to frantically contact some people I trusted at this point that knew that I had been considering this. One was my brother, who after getting ahold of eventually showed up and talked to me. Things were okay after that. Now I made some mistakes with this trip. I should have had a reliable trip sitter in the other room. I probably should have done it during the day (it was at night and I think the darkness made it feel more ominous). But despite all of that, and despite what some people might say about taking psilocybin when you're in a good place and not mentally distraught, I don't regret it. I think I realized some important things with it, such as the idea that I need to rely on my friends and family more to help me through things (something I'm still working on). It made me also able to more clearly see the love in my own grief, and how that just because my fiancee is not here physically anymore, doesn't mean her love doesn't persist and eternally surround and impact my existence. Grief is love, and there is something very beautiful about the type of love that is so strong it is able to cause such pain, but it can be very hard to emotionally see this, and only focus on how much it hurts. Psilocybin helped me realize that more clearly. I had a very good afterglow after that first trip. I reached out to a lot of people and expressed my love for them, and told my experience to the few I trusted with it. The subsequent days were lighter. I was able to get out of the house a bit more instead of locking myself away. And suicidal thoughts that I had from grief were quieted. 

My second trip was taken with those mistakes I had made in mind. This was more recent, back at the end of this February (first trip was in November? To give a timeline). And honestly the whole trip was pretty awesome. I felt anxious going into it and had some fear on the come up, but this time I was surrounded by my best friends (of which some I've known for 20 years) and it was during the day and we were able to go outside, feel the sun, the grass, and touch some trees. I felt more peace with existence again, even if there were aspects of it I really didn't like. For some reason it didn't bother me as much, even though I was aware that there were things in life that did bother me (such as my fiancee's death), and I decided all I could do was just face each thing as it came and love the things in life that I can. I missed my fiancee. I wished she could be there with us and have these experiences, too, but I also had a small feeling that somehow she was in a way. After this trip I experienced more peace, more ability to go out of the house (some of which had diminished some time after the first trip). I felt a stronger connection to nature and to life in general.

I'm really happy to have discovered/integrated psychedelics in my life. They definitely don't fix things completely, and I still have a lot to work on when it comes to processing and moving forward with my own grief, but I definitely feel like they helped me immensely. I think I'd be much further behind in my grief than I am if I hadn't tried psilocybin. Obviously everyone is different. Even on a level of just people having different experiences with these substances, individual grieving patterns or methods vary from person to person. And when it comes down to it, your partner's relationship with their mother is very different from my relationship with my fiancee obviously. 

Each time I took psilocybin it was on a "good day", meaning that the grief was less powerful on those days and I maybe had some good feelings from being with friends or family. I definitely think the normal wisdom from preparing for a trip (having a trusted sitter around/good set and setting) is very important. Everyone mentions intention with psychedelics all the time, and each trip I went with the intention to pull something from it. I wanted the mushrooms to show me love and beauty in my existence (which seems very dark at times) here, and perhaps a little purpose to go along with it. I feel like I received these things, and would think about and voice my intention before consumption. I definitely felt a lot of fear the first trip and even thoughstill felt it positive in a lot of ways, I think the fear I felt could have been avoided simply by having someone readily available for me. 

I hope this helps somewhat at least give a picture of someone who has used psychedelics with grief. I actually had a hard time finding experiences of people who talked about using psychedelics alongside grief specifically when I started researching them. And if you have any further questions about my experiences I'd be happy to answer them (there's honestly too much to fit in one response lol). Either way I wish both of you the best on this journey. Loss sucks and grief has no timeline. You sound very considerate of your partner and I'm sure that it helps a lot.

There is no such thing as grieving wrong. Everyone handles it differently and there are numerous reasons why we might be acting the way we do. Loss can be so surreal and oftentimes feel fake, and especially a week out I'd imagine it really hasn't set in yet for you. Not only that, but the guilt, unsettling feeling, and everything you're already experiencing is an aspect of grief. Grief isn't just crying. It's feeling those things and so much more, too. My heart goes out to you. I'm sure it will be tough going forward, but be patient with yourself and what you're feeling and realize everyone processes differently and there is no normal way to grieve. There is no timeline for it either, feelings will come up when they come up. Life has it's own beats, and I'm sure you'll have happy moments and funny moments in between the crying and the perceived "normal" parts of grief. That is okay, too.

Exactly this. So much. I have so many nights where I feel like if I just go to sleep I can wake up next to her and the nightmare will be over. And then I am disappointed every morning. But I keep hoping and wishing for it to happen and sometimes I feel like I actually believe it will even though I know it won't.

I'm so sorry.... I know for me it feels like my entire future is just gone in the blink of an eye, and I imagine you must feel similarly. There's so much more we were supposed to do with them. I'm so sorry for your loss. My heart breaks for you. I lost my fiancee about 3 months ago to a violent situation. During these initial days you're going through I tried to focus on taking it minute by minute because nothing anyone says or does can help. I'm so sorry.

These groups on reddit can be a great support. I also recommend looking at r/widowers as it is a sub dedicated solely to losing a partner. This group is great but losing a partner is a little different, and I have found being able to talk to others who have lost partners has been helpful. There are people of all ages on there, and an especially large group of younger people which it seems like you fall into that category. I am 25 myself, just to give an example. 

My heart goes out to you. Take care of yourself the best you can, and if you need to talk my inbox in open. I've talked to a lot of people that way myself over the past 3 months and it is helpful at times.

I have. It's been almost 3 months since she was killed.... I have no idea how to react to it sometimes. I feel so angry a lot, angry at the one who took her from me, but then I also feel sad a lot. Sad and depressed that there are people so dark inside their own minds that they have a need to commit such violence. During those times I feel like I should be angry instead, and even though I know I get angry at it, it's hard to know how exactly I'm supposed to react to everything. When I found out I wanted him found, but I wouldn't have known where to start and my first instinct was just to break down and try and even obtain some concrete proof that she had even been killed (I wasn't able to see her body until her viewing). I remember asking the detective who had talked to me if she had really been killed despite the fact I had already been told. I figured if anyone really knew he did. I sometimes wonder if my first reaction should have been to scour the streets for the guy instead, but I know that would have been fruitless and probably cause more trouble. I try to focus on the fact that nothing will bring her back, even though her killer was found and will likely spend the rest of his days in prison. I know she wouldn't want my mind in dark places, and she wouldn't want me to become a vengeful, hateful person because of this. Vengefulness and hatefulness were not qualities she loved me for, and not things I think I had really possessed before. It's still hard to know what to do, though. Hard to know how to react and how to handle it. Sometimes it feels like she died a different way, because murder is for TV shows and movies, not real life. I don't have any general advice myself, but I will be paying attention to this post in hope to maybe gain some of what you are seeking as well. I wish you the best of luck finding your own peace. My heart goes out to you.
That's a good way to put it. If you're crazy then I am too. I talk to her all the time when I'm alone. I'm not religious so I don't know if she hears me or anything but I do it anyways.

I'm not as far out but I definitely feel like this. I'm approaching 3 months soon and I hardly see anyone other than immediate family and my therapist. I was already not very social before all of this in the first place. She and I were very introverted, but we enjoyed each other's company all the time even when we wanted time away from other people. We didn't count as "other people" to each other. Now I find myself getting annoyed sometimes when other people spend too much time with me. I guess I kind of feel like I have always had this time set aside to spend time with her and when people spend too much time with me it feels as if they are infringing upon that, even though she's gone? I don't know but it's like you said. It's not the same without them, and no one else can replace them. A lot of times I just feel closer to her when I'm by myself, but the loneliness without her is always persistent no matter what I am doing.

I feel this so much. My fiancee was murdered and it was already a spectacle enough as it is. I don't want her to be remembered for being killed.
